title: Paddy’s Pub: The Worst Bar in Philadelphia

jokes.text: Charlie, the thinner the TV, the better the TV. That's just a straight-up fact.
jokes.setup: The gang is admiring a new flat-screen TV and debating its thinness.
jokes.punchline: Dennis delivers a completely circular, vacuous consumer logic as if it's axiomatic truth — the value of a thing IS the thing itself.
jokes.explanation: Classic Dennis logic — confident, status-obsessed, and entirely circular. It works because it perfectly captures his shallow materialism dressed up as wisdom. Good character integration but not especially novel.

jokes.text: "The first thing I noticed about Paddy's Pub is its charm. It has none."
jokes.setup: Mac reads the review aloud with excitement; everyone gets hopeful at "its charm."
jokes.punchline: "It has none" — a clean, brutal sentence-level reversal.
jokes.explanation: Structurally elegant: the sentence-level misdirection is executed with perfect economy — two words demolish all the hope built in the preceding clause. It's a crisp professional joke. The rewatch bonus comes from knowing the punchline is coming and savoring how the gang leans in.

jokes.text: "There was an ominous feeling that you could get stabbed at any moment." Dennis: "That's good, right?"
jokes.setup: The review describes the bar as feeling dangerously unsafe.
jokes.punchline: Dennis genuinely thinks this is a positive quality he cultivated intentionally.
jokes.explanation: Strong character integration — Dennis's pride in a dangerous atmosphere is completely on-brand. The gap between what a normal person would hear as a condemnation and what Dennis hears as validation is the core joke of the whole show distilled.

jokes.text: Dennis: "That's the exact type of atmosphere I've been trying to cultivate... like Swayze in Roadhouse. I'm the cooler."
jokes.setup: Dennis defends a stabbing-prone bar as his intentional vision.
jokes.punchline: He invokes Roadhouse and dubs himself "the cooler" — a grandiose self-image completely divorced from reality.
jokes.explanation: "I'm the cooler" becomes a running gag that pays off repeatedly throughout the episode. The Roadhouse reference is specific enough to feel earned rather than a random pop-culture drop — it's a real movie about bouncers, and Dennis genuinely believes he's Patrick Swayze, which is perfect character comedy.

jokes.text: "In check? There have been many stabbings in here. I feel unsafe here every single day."
jokes.setup: Dennis claims his bouncing abilities keep violence in check.
jokes.punchline: Charlie and Dee immediately and casually confirm that there have been MANY stabbings and they feel unsafe daily.
jokes.explanation: The casualness of the confirmation is the joke — not outrage, not fear, just matter-of-fact acceptance that their bar is a stabbing ground. Very Sunny in its worldbuilding.

jokes.text: Mac: "Well, stabbings have been down, though."
jokes.setup: Charlie and Dee confirm frequent stabbings and daily feeling of danger.
jokes.punchline: Mac's silver lining is that the stabbings are merely down — not gone — said with genuine pride.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — five words that do enormous work. The joke is entirely in the framing: Mac's bar is so violent that "stabbings are down" is actually meaningful progress, delivered with the quiet pride of a manager defending his quarterly metrics. Very quotable.

jokes.text: "Surly white trash waitress" — Dee's reaction and denial: "I am not white trash. I am a kind and a generous and a good-natured lady."
jokes.setup: Review describes the waitress as "surly white trash."
jokes.punchline: Dee's indignant self-description as kind, generous, and good-natured — immediately contradicted by everything we know about her and what she's about to say.
jokes.explanation: Classic Dee self-delusion. The triple adjective buildup (kind, generous, good-natured) is a good structural choice — it overcommits in a way that's inherently funny. Standard for the show but executed competently.

jokes.text: "I do seem to remember you calling a guy a faggot." Dee: "Yeah, I absolutely called him a faggot, but he ordered chardonnay. What was I supposed to do?"
jokes.setup: Dee insists she's a kind, good-natured lady.
jokes.punchline: She immediately confirms the slur with zero shame and provides a "justification" (he ordered chardonnay) that is itself the joke — the logic is insane and completely in character.
jokes.explanation: Structurally excellent: setup establishes Dee's self-image as a decent person, then she immediately and completely confirms the worst thing said about her — not reluctantly, but with pride and a baffling rationale. "What was I supposed to do?" as if there was no alternative is a perfect button. The chardonnay detail is a callback plant for later. This is genuinely good dark comedy writing.

jokes.text: Mac holds a hammer visibly while trying to convince Corman they are not white trash.
jokes.setup: The gang visits Corman to prove they're classy, not white trash.
jokes.punchline: Mac is conspicuously holding a hammer while claiming classiness, undercutting every word they say.
jokes.explanation: Classic visual irony — the gang arguing they're not threatening while one member holds a weapon. The joke works without a single word of acknowledgment, which is the sign of good visual comedy. Rewatch bonus because viewers catch new details about why Corman is alarmed.

jokes.text: "Don't let the hammer throw you, Corman. We are classy, interesting people."
jokes.setup: Corman is alarmed by Charlie's hammer. Mac and Dennis are there to prove they are classy.
jokes.punchline: Mac's attempt to dismiss the hammer alarm while still claiming classiness is completely oblivious.
jokes.explanation: 'Don't let the hammer throw you' is a great line because it treats a threatening prop as a minor social inconvenience. Confident obliviousness is Mac in a nutshell.

jokes.text: "You know what, buddy, we will jam your asshole up with so many lawyers, you won't know what to do with yourself."
jokes.setup: The gang threatens legal action for libel and slander.
jokes.punchline: Mac's legal threat devolves into the most anatomically graphic and legally meaningless metaphor imaginable.
jokes.explanation: Highly quotable. The escalation from legitimate-sounding legal language ("libel, slander") to an absurd anatomical threat is the structure of the joke. Mac's specific way of threatening — always physical, always slightly homoerotic — is perfectly in character.

jokes.text: "I'll have you know, we have a team of lawyers on retainer just to deal with people like you."
jokes.setup: Corman correctly notes libel only applies to falsehoods.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's completely fabricated claim of having a legal team — delivered with utter conviction — is an obvious lie told to a journalist.
jokes.explanation: Functional Dennis bluster. The gap between his claimed resources and reality is the standard Dennis joke. Competent but not exceptional.

jokes.text: "You're all out of time, bitch." / "Boom." / "You just got fazed." / "This just in, Poo-Poo Pants."
jokes.setup: Corman calls security on the gang, forcing them to leave.
jokes.punchline: Instead of leaving with dignity, they fire off a rapid salvo of made-up insults and self-congratulatory catchphrases as if they won the exchange.
jokes.explanation: "Poo-Poo Pants" and "fazed" are brilliant in their childishness — these grown adults think they're devastating with their parting shots. The gang's delusional sense of victory after being thrown out is perfectly Sunny. "Fazed" becomes a callback later, adding value.

jokes.text: "People don't read newspapers anymore. How's that for class?"
jokes.setup: The gang has just been humiliated and ejected from Corman's office.
jokes.punchline: Mac's parting shot — that newspapers are obsolete — is meant to be a withering final word but just reveals their total failure to land any real blow.
jokes.explanation: "How's that for class?" after the least classy exit imaginable is a nice self-undermining button. The joke works because the gang genuinely believes this was a power move.

jokes.text: The gang trying to hang a Blu-Ray player by dangling it, and Dee calling it 'very white trash.'
jokes.setup: Dennis bought expensive status-symbol electronics to prove they're not white trash.
jokes.punchline: Their installation solution is to 'dangle' the Blu-Ray player — immediately called out as 'very white trash' by Dee.
jokes.explanation: Good visual irony — buying expensive things to seem classy and immediately proving the opposite. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: "We'll just dangle it." / "That looks better." / "We're not dangling anything. That's very white trash."
jokes.setup: They have a Blu-ray player but no flat surface to put it on.
jokes.punchline: Charlie proposes dangling it; Mac agrees it looks better; Dee invokes "white trash" — the exact thing they're trying to avoid — as the critique.
jokes.explanation: The callback to the "white trash" label from the review gives this continuity. The visual of a dangling Blu-ray player is inherently funny. Competent escalation of the status anxiety theme.

jokes.text: "Holy shit. What? You kidnapped Corman?"
jokes.setup: Charlie says "I did something" and shows them something shocking.
jokes.punchline: The reveal that Charlie kidnapped the newspaper critic — following a simple angry/drinking sequence — is delivered with the casual horror of people who are only moderately surprised.
jokes.explanation: The reveal lands hard because kidnapping is a massive escalation over complaining about a bad review. What makes it Sunny-specific is that Mac and Dennis's reaction is not horror but pragmatic problem-solving mode — they're more annoyed than shocked, which tells us everything about these characters.

jokes.text: "First, I was angry. Then, I was drinking. Next thing I know, I'm following this guy home and forcing him into the trunk of his own car."
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis demand to know what happened.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's explanation is a perfect three-beat escalation with "then I was drinking" as the pivot that explains everything — delivered with no apparent awareness of how insane this is.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. The three-beat structure (angry → drinking → kidnapping) is comedy architecture at its finest — the middle beat does all the work, normalizing the leap to kidnapping as just what happens when Charlie drinks. The deadpan delivery and utter lack of shame is pure Charlie Kelly. Highly quotable and character-defining. Earns its 8+ score because it's structurally exceptional, not just shocking.

jokes.text: "Relax, I drove him around in a circle for a while, okay, so he wouldn't know where he was or how far away he'd gone."
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are panicking about the kidnapping.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's "reassurance" is that he drove in a circle — which is the dumbest possible version of obscuring a location — delivered as if this is a clever operational detail.
jokes.explanation: Charlie's criminal incompetence delivered as competence is a core comedy engine of the show. The circle detail is specific and visual enough to be genuinely funny.

jokes.text: "But then you brought him back to a place where he's already been, and plus, he just heard everything you just said."
jokes.setup: Charlie explains his circle-driving tactic as a smart move.
jokes.punchline: Dennis points out the double failure: (1) returned to a known location, (2) Corman heard the entire explanation.
jokes.explanation: The double-layer catch is well-structured. Dennis's role as the exasperated straight man who still isn't smart enough to fix anything is perfectly played here. The "he just heard everything" beat is a great comedic reveal.

jokes.text: "Maybe we can just release him, and that way, this won't be a kidnapping."
jokes.setup: Everyone is panicking about having committed kidnapping.
jokes.punchline: Mac's legal theory — that releasing someone retroactively removes the crime — is completely insane and delivered with apparent confidence.
jokes.explanation: Mac's legal reasoning is hilariously wrong in a very Mac way — he's always slightly confident in some misunderstood principle. The idea that the past can be unmade by present action is a recurring form of Sunny logic.

jokes.text: "Easy, we roll him up in a rug." / "Where are we gonna get a rug?" / "We buy a big Oriental rug." / "Do you have any idea how expensive rugs are, Charlie? Especially Oriental rugs."
jokes.setup: They need to smuggle Corman into the bar without being seen.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's rug solution is treated as logistically plausible right up until the expense is raised — no one objects to the insanity of the plan itself, only the rug cost.
jokes.explanation: The joke's genius is in what goes unchallenged: rolling a person in a rug is acceptable, but the EXPENSE is the dealbreaker. This is a perfect Sunny priorities joke — the gang's moral compass only points toward money. Very well-structured with a clear escalation and unexpected landing point.

jokes.text: "You're gonna be okay. It's not a kidnapping, so..."
jokes.setup: They're pulling Corman out of a trunk.
jokes.punchline: Mac's reassurance that "it's not a kidnapping" — said to a man they just extracted from a car trunk — is delivered as if this is genuinely comforting.
jokes.explanation: A callback to Mac's earlier legal theory, now applied in the most absurd real-world context. The trailing "so..." is perfectly chosen — it implies a resolution that isn't there.

jokes.text: "Just borrowing him."
jokes.setup: They're debating whether this counts as kidnapping.
jokes.punchline: "Just borrowing him" — the most domestically mundane reframing of abduction imaginable.
jokes.explanation: Three words, enormous comedic yield. The casualness of "borrowing" a human being is perfectly Sunny — it reframes an atrocity in the most banal possible terms. Very high economy score; nothing wasted.

jokes.text: "I'm pretty sure Charlie left with a trace." / "He probably did."
jokes.setup: They decide to go cover Charlie's tracks at Corman's apartment.
jokes.punchline: Dennis and Mac immediately agree that Charlie definitely left evidence everywhere — zero faith in Charlie's competence.
jokes.explanation: Quick, functional joke that plays on the established group dynamic. Mac's "He probably did" is a nice beat. Not exceptional but lands cleanly.

jokes.text: "Okay, but can we establish that I'm the cooler?" / "Oh, my God! Get into the bar." / "We're surrounded by idiots."
jokes.setup: In the middle of a kidnapping crisis, Dennis keeps trying to get official recognition as "the cooler."
jokes.punchline: He raises it again at the worst possible moment; Mac and Dee's exasperation is total.
jokes.explanation: The running gag pays off beautifully here because the gap between the stakes (active kidnapping) and Dennis's concern (official cooler status) is at its widest. "We're surrounded by idiots" from Dee is a perfect button that also applies to her own situation.

jokes.text: Charlie has Corman taped to a chair when Mac and Dee arrive.
jokes.setup: Mac tells Charlie not to do anything stupid while he's gone.
jokes.punchline: Charlie has gone immediately from "hold him" to full restraint situation.
jokes.explanation: Visual escalation — the situation has gotten materially worse in the time between scenes. Standard Sunny escalation engine.

jokes.text: "He sits around all day. He judges people with his words and his fancy newspaper talk. It's bullshit!"
jokes.setup: Mac asks Charlie why he taped Corman to a chair.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's grievance against a critic "judging with words" is an inadvertent description of literally all journalism — delivered with complete moral outrage.
jokes.explanation: "Fancy newspaper talk" is a great Charlie phrase — his outsider relationship to literacy and professional writing is core to the character. The indignation at being judged through the medium of words is hilariously specific.

jokes.text: "How can I write a new review if I am taped to a chair?"
jokes.setup: Charlie demands Corman write a new, less-critical review.
jokes.punchline: Corman's perfectly reasonable logical objection — delivered with weary flatness — highlights the total absurdity of the situation.
jokes.explanation: The straight-man's perfectly logical observation in an absurd situation. The delivery would be completely flat, which is exactly right. Corman as the deadpan foil to the gang's chaos is used well.

jokes.text: "He's twisting everything I say around. He's making me look like an asshole."
jokes.setup: Corman points out the logical impossibility of writing while restrained.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's complaint is that Corman is somehow distorting reality — when in fact, Charlie has kidnapped and taped a man to a chair.
jokes.explanation: One of the best examples of Charlie's self-victimization in the episode. He genuinely cannot see that he is the asshole, and blames Corman for accurately describing events. The lack of self-awareness is both hilarious and a perfect character note.

jokes.text: "I don't care. Let him piss in his pants." / "No, he can't piss in his pants, Charlie!" / "I don't know why you're so in love with this guy."
jokes.setup: Corman needs to use the bathroom but is taped down.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's completely reasonable (to him) solution; Mac objects on the grounds of kidnapping, not dignity; Charlie interprets Mac's decency as romantic interest.
jokes.explanation: Three-beat exchange that escalates beautifully. The triple-layer joke: (1) Charlie's casual cruelty, (2) Mac's pragmatic (not humanitarian) objection, (3) Charlie's jealousy accusation. "I don't know why you're so in love with this guy" is a perfect button — Charlie interprets basic decency as romantic rivalry. Very quotable.

jokes.text: "Nobody has to write anything against their will." — Corman: "Thank you." — "I have to go to the bathroom. I have to pee." — "Okay, sidebar."
jokes.setup: Mac tries to de-escalate by saying no one has to write anything against their will.
jokes.punchline: Corman immediately tries to leverage this goodwill to go to the bathroom, kicking off an absurd problem-chain about how a taped-up man pees.
jokes.explanation: Good setup for the bathroom escalation. 'Okay, sidebar' is a nice corporate-speak beat in the middle of a kidnapping. The momentum builds toward a bigger payoff.

jokes.text: "I used the last of the tape. If you untie him, that tape's not gonna stick back up."
jokes.setup: They consider untying Corman briefly to let him use the bathroom.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's objection to untying the kidnapping victim is entirely about duct tape re-usability, not any criminal consideration.
jokes.explanation: The tape reusability concern as the governing factor in a kidnapping negotiation is perfectly Charlie. His priorities are always slightly off in ways that reveal a unique but internally consistent worldview.

jokes.text: Mac's bouncer confrontation cutaway: "I saw that! You're out of here, bro."
jokes.setup: Mac is about to accompany Dennis to handle the "cooler" situation with Corman.
jokes.punchline: Brief cut to Mac ejecting someone from the bar — a completely irrelevant power display that is nevertheless clearly important to him.
jokes.explanation: Quick character beat that reinforces Mac's bouncer identity. The abruptness of the cut is itself the joke — he needed to do that regardless of what else was happening. Nice structure.

jokes.text: "Is he going to Cancun or Canada? You gotta pay attention to the details. This is how people get caught."
jokes.setup: Mac and Dee are packing Corman's apartment to fake a vacation.
jokes.punchline: Dennis lectures Mac and Dee about crime scene attention to detail — while they are actively committing multiple felonies — with the authority of someone who has done this before.
jokes.explanation: "Cancun or Canada" is a great alliterative pair that also works as a real diagnostic question. Dennis's crime expertise presented as management consultation is a great character beat — implies a dark backstory.

jokes.text: "He's probably under a lot of pressure with the deadlines from the newspaper. He should relax." / "Go someplace tropical?" / "Cancun then. Perfect."
jokes.setup: They're fabricating a reason for Corman to have "gone on vacation."
jokes.punchline: Mac and Dee begin genuinely sympathizing with their kidnapping victim's work stress while packing his bags for a fake trip.
jokes.explanation: The gap between their actions (covering up kidnapping) and their mindset (caring HR managers worried about their colleague's vacation) is beautifully absurd. Very Sunny in its casual evil-with-good-intentions tone.

jokes.text: Dee does a terrible Corman impression for the outgoing voicemail: "Hi, this is Mehar. Sorry I missed your call. Please leave a message after the beep. Peace."
jokes.setup: Dee puts a fake outgoing message on Corman's answering machine to sell the vacation cover story.
jokes.punchline: She (a) uses completely the wrong name (Mehar — the neighbor's), (b) adds "Peace" as a closing, and (c) Dennis simply says "That did not sound like Corman."
jokes.explanation: Multi-layered failure: wrong name, wrong vibe, wrong everything. The "Peace" closing is the crowning detail — it's so out of place it becomes its own joke. Dennis's dry three-word dismissal is a perfect button. This whole moment is Sunny comedy at its operational-incompetence best.

jokes.text: "Who are you people?" — Mehar discovers Mac and Dee in his neighbor's apartment.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dee are confidently staging a fake vacation in Corman's apartment.
jokes.punchline: They discover they're in the wrong apartment — it belongs to Mehar, who is now a witness.
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom escalation — the plan they were executing was flawed from the start (wrong apartment), and their self-satisfaction makes the reveal land harder. The acquisition of Mehar as a new problem character is a good structural choice.

jokes.text: "Normally, that wouldn't happen unless I wanted it to. 'Cause I could fire it right in your chest. 'Cause I got skills to do that."
jokes.setup: Dennis has just hit himself with his own pool cue while demonstrating his skills.
jokes.punchline: He immediately claims the self-injury was optional and pivots to a threat, trying to salvage his dignity.
jokes.explanation: "'Cause I got skills to do that" is an instant classic Dennis line. It's the perfect crystallization of his narcissistic refusal to acknowledge failure — not only was the injury voluntary, but the REAL threat was always to Corman's chest. The structure (injury → denial → threat) in rapid succession is beautifully compressed. This is as close to a Dennis Reynolds signature moment as the episode gets. The quotability is off the charts.

jokes.text: Mac and Charlie fight over a bandana, each arguing they found it / it was found for them.
jokes.setup: Charlie went to find more tape to re-restrain Corman; all he found was a small bandana.
jokes.punchline: Instead of acknowledging this is useless for restraint, they argue about WHO gets to wear the bandana they found in a crisis.
jokes.explanation: Good illustration of the gang's ability to get distracted by petty disputes during active crises. The bandana ownership dispute is appropriately absurd given the circumstances.

jokes.text: "In fact it's so clean I would say you could eat out of these urinals."
jokes.setup: Corman says the bathroom is disgusting; Charlie defends his cleaning work.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's benchmark for cleanliness is that you could eat from the urinals — which is insane but delivered with genuine janitor's pride.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Charlie Kelly moment. The character's specific relationship to the bar's maintenance — his pride in cleaning combined with his genuinely degraded standards — is the core of the joke. "Eat out of these urinals" as a cleanliness benchmark is both horrifying and deeply specific to Charlie. Character integration score near-perfect because no other character on any show would say this. Sets up the immediate physical payoff.

jokes.text: Charlie eats something out of the urinal to prove his point, while Mac protests and Corman reacts in horror.
jokes.setup: Charlie claims you could eat from the urinals; Corman says no you absolutely could not.
jokes.punchline: Charlie immediately eats from the urinal. Then Mac reveals he pissed in there five minutes earlier.
jokes.explanation: One of the strongest jokes in the episode. The structure is exceptional: claim → immediate physical proof → retroactive horror (Mac's revelation). The triple escalation (Charlie eats it, Mac reveals he urinated in it, Charlie continues chewing to prove his point) is a masterclass in Sunny escalation. The fact that Charlie KEEPS CHEWING after the revelation is the apex. High impact because the audience knows what's coming once Charlie reaches for the urinal, but the Mac detail resets the horror fresh. The 'You're still chewing it' callback is devastating.

jokes.text: "Well, I think one of us is gonna have to help his..." "Whoa, dude! I'm not touching his dick." / "Well, Charlie, you're the one that used all the tape."
jokes.setup: Corman agrees to write the review in exchange for being allowed to use the bathroom, but his hands are still taped down.
jokes.punchline: The logical implication of helping him use the bathroom hits Mac mid-sentence; Dennis's response is to shift moral responsibility to Charlie via the tape.
jokes.explanation: The mid-sentence realization is well-timed comedy — Mac starts to say it and stops himself when he realizes what he's describing. Dennis's "you used all the tape" as a moral calculus for who should touch their captive's genitals is a great absurdist-logic moment. Sets up the even funnier aftermath.

jokes.text: "Well, all right, fine. Then compromise. We'll both do it. That way it's equally weird for both of us."
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie argue about who has to assist Corman in the bathroom.
jokes.punchline: Mac's compromise — both doing it simultaneously to distribute the weirdness equally — is somehow even worse than either individual option.
jokes.explanation: "That way it's equally weird for both of us" is a top-tier Sunny line. Mac applies an entirely rational fairness framework to an utterly irrational situation, arriving at an outcome that is objectively far worse. The logic is internally consistent and completely insane. Highly quotable in multiple contexts.

jokes.text: Corman gets a little aroused while Mac and Charlie help him in the bathroom. Post-scene: "Did he get a little bit hard on us?" / "Can we not talk about this?" / "Well, why did it move?!"
jokes.setup: Mac and Charlie reluctantly agreed to help Corman use the bathroom while restrained.
jokes.punchline: They return traumatized and are immediately arguing about an involuntary physiological response, with Dennis demanding an explanation for "why did it move."
jokes.explanation: "Why did it move?!" is an instant-quotable, devastating line. The structure is excellent: cut away from the worst part, return to the aftermath and trauma. Dennis's baffled indignation at involuntary physiology is the perfect button. This is one of the episode's best cringe payoffs — it doesn't show anything but lets the audience's imagination do the work, which is smarter than showing it. High impact because the audience has been dreading/anticipating this return.

jokes.text: "It's a classic mistake" — Charlie's response to being told you can't kidnap more people to cover up the original kidnapping.
jokes.setup: Mac tells Charlie you can't kidnap multiple people to cover up the first kidnapping.
jokes.punchline: "It's a classic mistake" — said as if serial kidnapping cover-up attempts are a known pitfall that reasonable people fall into.
jokes.explanation: "It's a classic mistake" is an outstanding line — it implies that there is an established body of knowledge about kidnapping cover-up attempts that everyone should know to avoid. The normalization of serial kidnapping as a known error type is both hilarious and deeply character-specific. Very high economy — four words, tremendous payoff. Mac's "I didn't know there was a handbook on kidnapping" is a good counter but slightly weakens by over-explaining.

jokes.text: "I'm sorry, I didn't know there was a handbook on kidnapping."
jokes.setup: Charlie says "it's a classic mistake" about kidnapping more people.
jokes.punchline: Mac's sarcastic response implies Charlie's confident expertise implies the existence of kidnapping literature.
jokes.explanation: A good response but slightly over-explains the previous joke. The sarcasm works but it's one beat more than needed after the perfect "classic mistake." Still gets a laugh.

jokes.text: "He started asking questions." — Mehar: "I asked one question." — "Shut up! No, you asked a lot of questions."
jokes.setup: Mac explains why they had to take Mehar — he was asking questions.
jokes.punchline: Mehar quietly corrects that he asked exactly one question. Mac defensively insists it was many questions.
jokes.explanation: Good small beat. Mehar's quiet, precise correction versus Mac's bluster is a nice straight-man moment. Economical and character-revealing.

jokes.text: "There's another bit of an issue, which is that I locked the keys in the trunk just now."
jokes.setup: They have a man locked in a car trunk in public.
jokes.punchline: Charlie has locked the car keys in the trunk with him — a new, compounding disaster.
jokes.explanation: Classic Sunny escalation — adding new, preventable disasters on top of existing ones. "Well, I didn't want to bring that up" is a nice understated delivery choice.

jokes.text: "How long do you think we can hold that inside?" / "It's burning me up inside. It's burning me up."
jokes.setup: Everyone just went inside without discussing the bathroom incident.
jokes.punchline: Mac and Charlie immediately confirm they cannot contain their trauma and need to discuss "the thing" — delivered with the urgency of people who witnessed something unspeakable.
jokes.explanation: "It's burning me up inside" from Charlie about an incident they just agreed not to discuss is a good sustained cringe beat. Extends the emotional aftermath of the bathroom scene effectively.

jokes.text: "There he is. Our little typer. Type, type, typing away."
jokes.setup: Dennis and Dee approach Corman, who is writing at a desk after everything that's happened.
jokes.punchline: Dennis greets their kidnapping victim with the warmth of a proud uncle watching his nephew do homework.
jokes.explanation: "Our little typer" is a perfect Dennis line — the possessive, the diminutive, the affectionate tone toward someone he's holding against their will. It's character-specific and very quotable.

jokes.text: "No, that wasn't us. That was somebody else's idea." / "Not our idea."
jokes.setup: Dennis and Dee apologize to Corman for "the tie-up-and-hold-you-here thing."
jokes.punchline: They immediately clarify they had nothing to do with it — to the man they are literally holding captive, in their own bar.
jokes.explanation: Their transparent self-exculpation to the person they kidnapped is a good irony beat. The parallel denial delivery works well.

jokes.text: "Yeah, how about, uh, letting me go." Dennis and Dee laugh: "There he goes again. I didn't know he was so funny."
jokes.setup: Dennis and Dee ask if there's anything they can do for Corman.
jokes.punchline: He asks to be released; they treat this as a quirky comedic catchphrase rather than a reasonable request.
jokes.explanation: The gap between Corman's desperation and the gang's reading of it as charming wit is perfectly executed. "I didn't know he was so funny" from Dee is great — she's genuinely delighted.

jokes.text: "A glass of white wine, maybe a chardonnay." Dee immediately: "Um, also, do you want me to bring you some lipstick with that?"
jokes.setup: Dennis and Dee ask what they can get Corman; he orders chardonnay.
jokes.punchline: Dee immediately fires the chardonnay/masculinity slur from the opening scene.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed callback — the chardonnay detail planted in the opening review scene pays off here. Corman ordering chardonnay is almost certainly intentional (he's testing or mocking Dee), making Dee's reflexive response funnier and her total self-unawareness complete. Dennis's line "You can't just tee her up and expect her not to take a swing" perfectly frames the callback's logic. This is craft-level callback work.

jokes.text: "Boom! You got fazed again, Corman."
jokes.setup: Dee insults Corman with the lipstick comment.
jokes.punchline: "Fazed" callback from the earlier Corman confrontation scene.
jokes.explanation: The "fazed" running gag gets its second payoff. Shorter this time — just the word with "Boom" — which is correct; the first instance was the full joke, this is the condensed callback version.

jokes.text: "You can't just tee her up and expect her not to take a swing at you, right?" / "Can't blame her for that one."
jokes.setup: Corman ordered chardonnay and Dee immediately insulted him.
jokes.punchline: Dennis and Mac frame Dee's reflexive homophobic insult as an understandable defensive reaction — "teeing her up" — as if Corman provoked it by ordering wine.
jokes.explanation: The gang closing ranks around each other's worst behavior is thematically core to the show. The sports metaphor (tee her up / take a swing) is a nice framing for the insult.

jokes.text: "Hey, since you are writing a new review, uh, is there anything I can do to help you out with it?... I just want to make sure you got the total picture on me 'cause I do drive a Range Rover."
jokes.setup: Dennis offers to assist Corman with his review.
jokes.punchline: His idea of contributing to journalism about their kidnapping bar is to mention he drives a Range Rover.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Dennis vanity. His contribution to a kidnapping-adjacent review is vehicle-based status signaling. "I do drive a Range Rover" as a journalistic addendum is extremely specific and character-perfect.

jokes.text: "Gas guzzler." / "Well, not on the highway. Okay."
jokes.setup: Dennis brags about his Range Rover.
jokes.punchline: Corman's one-word dismissal prompts Dennis to pivot to highway fuel efficiency — a completely defensive and undignified response.
jokes.explanation: Corman's "Gas guzzler" is two words that completely demolish Dennis's status claim. Dennis's "not on the highway" is an outstanding character choice — he doesn't deny it, he quibbles with the technicality. Perfect economy on both sides.

jokes.text: "Dennis Reynolds, your car is awesome. Your flat screen TV... I took a look at it. It's very, very thin. It speaks volumes about you as a person."
jokes.setup: Dennis asks Corman what he wants him to write about him.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's ideal review is a word-for-word endorsement of his thin TV and car — the very things he was defending at the episode's start. His review of himself is essentially "very thin TV man."
jokes.explanation: A satisfying full-circle callback to the cold open. Dennis's ideal press is thin-TV validation — it reveals his entire worldview: status objects as identity, external validation as purpose. "It speaks volumes about you as a person" about a TV thickness is a perfect absurdist endpoint. This is good structural writing at the episode level.

jokes.text: "I don't drink scotch." Dee: "Well, you don't have to be a dick about it."
jokes.setup: Dee brings Corman scotch because she thinks that's what writers drink.
jokes.punchline: Corman's simple preference refusal is treated by Dee as an act of aggression.
jokes.explanation: Dee's hair-trigger offense at the slightest rebuff is very in-character. The irony of accusing a kidnapping victim of being a dick for not liking scotch is good. "Got a real chip on her shoulder" from Dennis is a nice follow-up.

jokes.text: "The headline might be: 'Most negative man in the world calls other people white trash to make himself not feel so faggy'."
jokes.setup: Dee claims she'd write an article about how negative Corman is.
jokes.punchline: Her proposed headline is pure id — gratuitous, confused in its own logic, and so specifically Dee that it circles back around to character comedy.
jokes.explanation: It's a Dee moment — unhinged, self-undermining (she's the white trash), and delivered with conviction. The headline structure gives it a punchy frame. The word choice is Dee-specific in its graceless aggression.

jokes.text: "It's, uh, pretty heavy on the kidnapping aspect."
jokes.setup: Mac sneaks a look at what Corman has been typing for his "new review."
jokes.punchline: Mac's review of the review is a devastating understatement — the article is apparently focused on the kidnapping rather than the bar's rebranding.
jokes.explanation: "Pretty heavy on the kidnapping aspect" is an outstanding understatement — it treats "wrote about being kidnapped" as a minor editorial imbalance. The delivery word "pretty" (not 'extremely,' not 'mostly') is exactly right. Very quotable in the right contexts.

jokes.text: Mac's roundhouse kick attempt to break the car window — he misses badly and falls, breaking the side mirror instead.
jokes.setup: Mac declares he will roundhouse kick the car window to free Mehar. Charlie is skeptical. Mac has never been more serious about anything.
jokes.punchline: Mac misses, falls, and breaks the side mirror instead — blaming the slope in the ground.
jokes.explanation: Classic Mac physical comedy — his confidence in his own fighting abilities vs. complete incompetence. "I've never been more serious about anything in my entire life" followed by a spectacularly failed kick is perfect setup/payoff. The mirror-instead-of-window detail is a good specific twist. His excuse ("the street's slope") is a great character beat.

jokes.text: "Charlie, I've never been more serious about anything in my entire life."
jokes.setup: Charlie is skeptical that Mac can break a car window with a roundhouse kick.
jokes.punchline: Mac's earnest, grave sincerity about an objectively absurd claim — delivered with complete conviction — is both the setup for the physical gag and a joke in its own right.
jokes.explanation: "I've never been more serious about anything in my entire life" spoken about a roundhouse kick is an outrageously proportionate statement that reveals Mac's entire character: physical combat as sacred calling. Very quotable in many contexts.

jokes.text: "Sir, we all have cats that we'd like to be playing with right now, okay? We're doing our very best."
jokes.setup: Mehar, locked in the trunk, pleads to be released because his diabetic cat needs insulin.
jokes.punchline: Mac addresses Mehar's cat emergency by suggesting that everyone has recreational cat interests they're sacrificing — as if playing with a cat and giving a diabetic cat insulin are equivalent preferences.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. The moral equivalence drawn between "I'd like to play with a cat" and "my cat will die without insulin" is a spectacular miscalibration. Mac's sincere empathy-framing ("we all") while delivering a completely tone-deaf response is excellent character comedy. "We're doing our very best" is perfect, earnest management-speak for 'we trapped you in a trunk.' Highly quotable.

jokes.text: "Learn how to kick. Take one karate class if you're so into karate, you know?"
jokes.setup: Mac has just failed spectacularly at a roundhouse kick and left.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's perfectly measured advice — if you're going to claim karate skills, maybe take a single class.
jokes.explanation: "Take one karate class" is the right level of insult — not elaborate, just devastating in its reasonableness. Charlie occasionally gets to be the voice of practical common sense, which is funny coming from him.

jokes.text: "A diabetic cat is in play? Jesus, we can't catch a break."
jokes.setup: Mac arrives back with Mehar's cat, which is diabetic and needs insulin.
jokes.punchline: Dennis frames a diabetic cat needing insulin as the universe personally victimizing them, rather than a consequence of kidnapping two people.
jokes.explanation: "We can't catch a break" is a great self-victimization line from people who made every bad decision. The cat being diabetic specifically is a good absurdist detail — not just a cat but a cat with a medical condition.

jokes.text: "Dude, your cat's freaking out!" / "That's not my cat." / "What?!"
jokes.setup: Mac arrives with what he thinks is Mehar's diabetic cat.
jokes.punchline: It's not Mehar's cat. No one is sure whose cat it is.
jokes.explanation: Good chaos escalation — a third unexpected problem element added to the pile. The wrong-cat reveal is a good quick gag.

jokes.text: "What the hell you doin', Dee?" / "What is going on?" Charlie window-smash reveal: "Dude, the guy had to take a dump. What was I supposed to do?" / "Wait, he's all tied up. How did you...?" / "Let's not talk about how it happened, okay? It just happened."
jokes.setup: Mac left Charlie in charge of Corman; Dennis left to deal with the car; total chaos has ensued.
jokes.punchline: The car window is broken. Charlie's explanation — the captive had to defecate — raises more questions than it answers, which Charlie refuses to address.
jokes.explanation: "Let's not talk about how it happened, okay? It just happened." is an outstanding line — a pure defense against further questioning, refusing to acknowledge that "it just happened" does no explanatory work. The audience is left imagining the logistics, which is funnier than showing them. Perfect Charlie solution to an impossible situation.

jokes.text: Charlie's amnesia plan: "Okay, we give them amnesia. It's so easy, here how you do it. You smash them both over the head with a bottle... we set their clocks back. We get yesterday's newspaper. We put it on their front doorstep. They wake up thinking it was all a dream."
jokes.setup: The gang needs a plan to escape the multi-kidnapping situation.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's plan is an elaborate movie-logic amnesia scheme involving bottling two people, resetting clocks, and staging yesterday's newspaper — delivered as the obvious solution.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The plan is elaborate, internally detailed, and entirely based on cartoon logic — but Charlie presents it with the confidence of someone who has clearly worked this out before. The specificity (clocks back, yesterday's newspaper on the doorstep) escalates the absurdity with each detail. The final step — "they wake up thinking it was all a dream" — is delivered as a logical conclusion. Dennis's response ("That's so goddamn stupid") is the right beat. This is excellent character-specific absurdist comedy.

jokes.text: "I say... we bribe them." / "A good, old-fashioned bribe."
jokes.setup: Charlie's amnesia plan is rejected; Mac offers an alternative.
jokes.punchline: "A good, old-fashioned bribe" — said with the relief of returning to sensible, familiar criminal territory.
jokes.explanation: "Good, old-fashioned" is the right qualifier — it implies bribery is their home base, the comfortable option. Functional rather than exceptional.

jokes.text: "I touch his dick. Mac, we touched his dick."
jokes.setup: In the middle of negotiating a deal with Corman, Mac blurts out the unprocessed bathroom trauma.
jokes.punchline: The timing — during a formal legal negotiation — and the phrasing ("we touched his dick" as shared ownership of the act) is perfectly wrong.
jokes.explanation: "Mac, we touched his dick" is one of the most quotable lines of the episode. The bluntness, the mid-negotiation timing, the "we" (implicating Dennis in what was really Mac and Charlie's decision), and the absolute inability to maintain professionalism make this exceptional. High quotability score — this line becomes a shorthand reference for the episode.

jokes.text: "Now is not the time to talk about that." Charlie: "Why were you guys touching his dick?" Dennis: "There wasn't enough tape and..." / "So you touched his dick?!" / "Move past it. Let's plow through it."
jokes.setup: Mac blurts out the dick-touching revelation in the middle of a negotiation.
jokes.punchline: The whole exchange breaks down as Charlie asks for details, Dennis accidentally confirms more, and Mac tries to end it.
jokes.explanation: The "there wasn't enough tape" explanation as the logical chain leading to genital contact is a brilliantly compressed piece of Sunny plotting. Charlie's innocent curiosity (he wasn't there) getting the worst possible answers is well-structured. "Let's plow through it" has an inadvertent double meaning that's surely intentional.

jokes.text: "Now, we won't charge you for the duct tape. That was a joke."
jokes.setup: Dennis finishes the release paperwork and removes Corman's tape.
jokes.punchline: He announces he won't charge for the duct tape used to restrain the kidnapping victim, then has to clarify "that was a joke" — implying he either couldn't tell or the room was too silent.
jokes.explanation: The "that was a joke" follow-up is what makes it land — it implies that everyone's default assumption was that Dennis might actually charge for the tape, which tells you everything about how they read him. Good character-specific meta-comedy.

jokes.text: Charlie smashes the bottle over Corman's head immediately after the deal is struck.
jokes.setup: The gang has just successfully negotiated Corman's release and non-prosecution. The crisis appears resolved.
jokes.punchline: Charlie immediately executes part of his rejected amnesia plan — bottling Corman — right after the resolution.
jokes.explanation: One of the best gags in the episode. The amnesia plan was established, explicitly rejected ("that's so goddamn stupid"), and then executed anyway, immediately after a successful diplomatic resolution. The absence of any buildup — Charlie just does it — is what makes it exceptional. It's pure Charlie: he planned the solution, he still believes in it, he's going to implement it regardless. The structure is perfect: plan introduced → rejected → tension resolved via other means → plan executed anyway. Highest earned_vs_cheap score because it's completely set up.

jokes.text: "You idiot!" / "Well, we'll see who's the idiot when he wakes up tomorrow and doesn't remember a thing." / "I don't think that's how it works." / "It's definitely not how it works, man."
jokes.setup: Charlie has just bottled Corman, undoing the resolution.
jokes.punchline: Charlie remains completely confident in the amnesia science — everyone else correctly notes this is not how concussions work.
jokes.explanation: "We'll see who's the idiot" from Charlie — spoken as if amnesia results are verifiable the next morning — is a great line. Mac and Dennis's parallel rejection ("I don't think" / "It's definitely not") is good structure.

jokes.text: "We may as well embrace the amnesia angle, because we have no other options at this point." / "Well, now!" / "Okay, I'll go get yesterday's newspaper."
jokes.setup: Corman is now unconscious; they have no other plan.
jokes.punchline: Mac's reluctant acceptance of Charlie's plan is immediately greeted with excited vindication; Charlie goes for the newspaper with no hesitation.
jokes.explanation: "Well, now!" from Charlie — his vindicated excitement — is the perfect character note. He was right all along in his own mind and his enthusiasm is completely unironic. "Okay, I'll go get yesterday's newspaper" is matter-of-fact and shows he had already planned exactly where to get it.

jokes.text: The gang sings a full a cappella farewell to Corman while he is unconscious: a slow, earnest harmony performance.
jokes.setup: They are performing the amnesia plan — staging the apartment, getting the newspaper. Part of the plan involves, apparently, a musical send-off.
jokes.punchline: The gang performs a full, sincere, harmonized a cappella song to their unconscious kidnapping victim as a farewell gesture, apparently as a natural part of their plan.
jokes.explanation: The tonal whiplash is the joke — these genuinely terrible people, who have just assaulted a journalist, are sending him off with a sincere, earnest vocal performance. The fact that they appear to be legitimately trying to sing well, with harmony, makes it funnier. Charlie running out of breath is a good button. It's also slightly unsettling, which is the perfect Sunny register.

jokes.text: "I woke up in my neighbor's bed with a head wound, yesterday's paper, and an empty bottle of sleeping pills..."
jokes.setup: Mac reads Corman's new, published review.
jokes.punchline: The amnesia plan failed — Corman remembers everything and wrote the review of his actual experience: waking up in a strange bed, injured, with props staged around him.
jokes.explanation: The amnesia plan's failure is the final structural payoff of the episode's main comedic thread. "Yesterday's paper and an empty bottle of sleeping pills" as staged props that did nothing are great details. The review being MORE damning than the original is a satisfying escalation endpoint.

jokes.text: "The owners all deserve to rot in jail, though having to spend every day with each other in that violent establishment is a decidedly great punishment."
jokes.setup: Corman explains why he's not pressing charges.
jokes.punchline: Spending time with each other is explicitly worse than jail — the ultimate dark roast of the gang's dynamic.
jokes.explanation: A structurally elegant final observation that serves as the episode's thematic thesis: the gang IS each other's punishment. The phrasing is clean and the logic is unimpeachable. Earns its score as a genuinely good piece of writing that works on both the comedic and thematic level.

jokes.text: "At least, he didn't mention our names." Then immediate: "I don't know why, but I'm a little irritated that he didn't mention our names."
jokes.setup: The gang reads the devastating final review — no charges, but complete condemnation.
jokes.punchline: Their only remaining concern is the lack of name recognition — after everything that happened, they wanted the publicity.
jokes.explanation: One of the best episode-closing jokes. The pivot from relief ("at least no names") to irritation ("I'm a little irritated he didn't mention our names") in a single beat is a perfect expression of the gang's unquenchable ego. Their desire for recognition outweighs their relief at escaping prosecution. This is the show's thesis statement about its characters delivered as a punchline. The specificity of "a little irritated" (not outraged — just mildly annoyed) is exactly right.

jokes.text: "We're capable of being civils, right?" / "Communication is the key, it make sens." / They head back to confront Corman again — with the hammer.
jokes.setup: The gang decides to confront Corman again about not mentioning their names.
jokes.punchline: The episode ends with them repeating the exact behavior that caused all the problems — going to confront the critic, hammer in hand — having learned absolutely nothing.
jokes.explanation: Perfect structural closing. The hammer, which was the visual gag establishing their lack of class in the confrontation scene, reappears as the episode's final image. The gang has gone through an entire kidnapping ordeal and their primary grievance is not getting their names in the paper. The circular structure (they're doing the exact same thing again) is both the comedic and thematic endpoint of the show's premise: these people cannot change and cannot learn. "Communication is the key" said while heading to confront someone with a hammer is a lovely final ironic grace note.

tmdb_overview: A newspaper critic is kidnapped by the gang after he calls Paddy's pub the worst bar in Philadelphia.
